Tables: rows of exception / action / owner tables are separate cases; extract each row's
condition, action and owner as their own claims.
Only create a relation when the sequence is supported by wording or structure.
Keep source conflicts separate with a SOURCE_CONFLICT issue.
Flag missing sections and references to other pages as SOURCE_INCOMPLETE.
All IDs you create must start with "T" (e.g. T_actor1, T_c1, T_r1).

1. Purpose, Scope and Dispute Categories
1.1 Purpose
Provide a consistent, fair, traceable process for investigating card transaction disputes. The process should protect customers, reduce
avoidable losses, meet applicable deadlines, preserve evidence, and ensure decisions are made by authorised staff.
1.2 Scope
The process begins when a customer reports a card transaction they believe is incorrect or unauthorised. It ends when the case is
resolved, any required adjustment is posted, the customer is informed, and the record is closed or transferred to a controlled recovery
process.
• Included: intake, authentication, transaction lookup, dispute categorisation, evidence collection, investigation, eligibility and

[E4] (SOP_debit_card_dispute_chargeback.pdf, page 2)
deadline checks, chargeback or other remedy assessment, customer updates, adjustments, and case closure.
• Excluded: card issuance, card replacement as a standalone process, merchant acquiring operations, legal proceedings, and
detailed scheme-specific technical instructions.
• Channels may include secure online banking, phone, branch, or another approved customer-service channel.
1.3 Common dispute categories
Category Example Initial handling focus
Unauthorised transaction Customer says they did not make or
permit the payment.
Secure the account/card as appropriate;
assess fraud indicators and customer
authentication.
Duplicate transaction The same purchase appears to have
been charged twice.
Compare references, dates, amounts,
and transaction status.

amount.

Goods/services issue Goods not received or materially different

Collect order, delivery, cancellation, and
merchant-contact evidence as applicable.
Cash withdrawal dispute Customer disputes an ATM cash
withdrawal.
Review ATM records, dispense/reversal
status, and relevant logs.
1.4 Core principles
• Treat the customer respectfully and avoid promising an outcome before investigation.
• Use approved identity verification and secure case-management systems.

[E6] (SOP_debit_card_dispute_chargeback.pdf, page 2)
• Apply the correct dispute category and deadline rules; do not assume all categories have the same process.
• Protect sensitive data and restrict access to staff with a business need.
• Keep evidence, decisions, timestamps, and communications auditable.

Where required, the person who prepares a financial adjustment must not be the sole person approving it. Higher-value adjustments,

2.2 Staff conduct and access
• Use individual credentials and approved systems only.

STANDARD OPERATING PROCEDURE
Retail Banking — Debit Card Dispute and Chargeback Handling
Document control Details
Document ID OPS-CARD-DSP-002 (fictional example)
Version / status Version 1.0 — Training draft
Effective date 12 October 2026 (illustrative)
Process owner Card Operations Manager (role title)
Review cycle Annually and after material incidents, scheme-rule changes, or
system changes
Classification Internal training example — not an approved bank procedure
Purpose
This SOP sets out a controlled workflow for receiving, investigating, deciding, and resolving a retail customer’s debit-card transaction
dispute, including potential unauthorised transactions, duplicate charges, incorrect amounts, and goods or services disputes.
Important notice

This is a fictional, generic training document. It is not issued or approved by any bank and must not be used as an operational
procedure. Actual handling must follow the institution’s approved policies, applicable law, card-scheme rules, customer terms, and
dispute time limits.

Page 2
1. Purpose, Scope and Dispute Categories
1.1 Purpose
Provide a consistent, fair, traceable process for investigating card transaction disputes. The process should protect customers, reduce
avoidable losses, meet applicable deadlines, preserve evidence, and ensure decisions are made by authorised staff.
1.2 Scope
The process begins when a customer reports a card transaction they believe is incorrect or unauthorised. It ends when the case is
resolved, any required adjustment is posted, the customer is informed, and the record is closed or transferred to a controlled recovery
process.
• Included: intake, authentication, transaction lookup, dispute categorisation, evidence collection, investigation, eligibility and

deadline checks, chargeback or other remedy assessment, customer updates, adjustments, and case closure.
• Excluded: card issuance, card replacement as a standalone process, merchant acquiring operations, legal proceedings, and
detailed scheme-specific technical instructions.
• Channels may include secure online banking, phone, branch, or another approved customer-service channel.
1.3 Common dispute categories
Category Example Initial handling focus
Unauthorised transaction Customer says they did not make or
permit the payment.
Secure the account/card as appropriate;
assess fraud indicators and customer
authentication.
Duplicate transaction The same purchase appears to have
been charged twice.
Compare references, dates, amounts,
and transaction status.

Incorrect amount Posted amount differs from the expected
amount.
Compare receipt, authorisation, clearing
record, and currency conversion details.
Cancelled or returned purchase Merchant credit/refund has not appeared. Request cancellation/refund evidence
and check processing timelines.
Goods/services issue Goods not received or materially different
from what was agreed.
Collect order, delivery, cancellation, and
merchant-contact evidence as applicable.
Cash withdrawal dispute Customer disputes an ATM cash
withdrawal.
Review ATM records, dispense/reversal
status, and relevant logs.
1.4 Core principles
• Treat the customer respectfully and avoid promising an outcome before investigation.
• Use approved identity verification and secure case-management systems.

• Apply the correct dispute category and deadline rules; do not assume all categories have the same process.
• Protect sensitive data and restrict access to staff with a business need.
• Keep evidence, decisions, timestamps, and communications auditable.

Page 3
2. Roles and Responsibilities
Role Responsibilities Key control
Customer / cardholder Reports the transaction, confirms details,
and supplies requested evidence.
Verify identity before disclosing account
or case information.
Customer Service Officer Receives report, authenticates customer,
records facts, and explains next steps.
Must not promise a refund or disclose
unverified information.
Card Disputes Analyst Categorises case, checks deadlines,
gathers evidence, investigates and
recommends an outcome.
Use the approved checklist and record a
reasoned decision.
Fraud Operations Assesses potential account compromise,
suspicious patterns, and protective
action.
Follow approved fraud procedures;
document account/card controls applied.

Card Operations Checker / Supervisor Independently reviews decisions,
adjustments, and cases requiring
additional approval.
Separate preparation from approval
where policy requires.
Payments / Reconciliation Team Verifies posting, reversal, refund,
provisional credit, and final adjustment
entries.
Investigate mismatches; do not manually
force-match entries.
Compliance / Legal (when needed) Advises on regulatory, privacy, complaint,
or legal escalation requirements.
Only authorised staff determine legally
sensitive handling.
Case Management System Stores case status, deadlines,
documents, notes, decisions, and audit
trail.
Role-based access and reliable
timestamps are required.
2.1 Segregation of duties

Where required, the person who prepares a financial adjustment must not be the sole person approving it. Higher-value adjustments,
policy exceptions, or sensitive cases must follow the bank’s delegated authority matrix.
2.2 Staff conduct and access
• Use individual credentials and approved systems only.
• Do not ask customers to send full card security codes or passwords.
• Do not store customer evidence on personal devices or unapproved shared drives.
• Escalate suspected fraud, data exposure, threats, or control bypass through the approved incident route.

Page 4
3. Receive the Dispute and Register the Case
3.1 Intake procedure
1. Receive the report through an approved channel and confirm the customer’s identity using the channel’s authentication
procedure.
2. Locate the relevant card account and transaction using approved systems.
3. Create a unique dispute case ID and record the date and time received, channel, customer identifier, and officer handling the
case.
4. Capture the customer’s description in their own words where practical, including why the transaction is disputed and when they
first noticed it.
5. Confirm whether the customer recognises the merchant, location, amount, date, and transaction type without leading the
customer toward a particular answer.

6. Check whether a related fraud report, previous dispute, merchant refund, reversal, or open case already exists.
3.2 Minimum case information
Information Requirement
Customer and card account Identify the correct customer and account using approved
internal identifiers; avoid unnecessary exposure of full card
details.
Transaction details Transaction reference, merchant, date, amount, currency,
status, and transaction channel where available.
Dispute reason Customer’s explanation and selected category; note any
uncertainty.
Supporting evidence Receipt, order confirmation, cancellation confirmation, merchant
correspondence, ATM details, or other relevant evidence,
depending on case type.
Contact and consent records Verified contact route and any required customer declarations

or acknowledgements.
Risk and protection flags Possible card compromise, suspicious activity, customer
vulnerability, or urgent account-protection needs according to
policy.
3.3 Protect the customer where necessary
If the report suggests a stolen card, compromised credentials, or ongoing unauthorised activity, follow the approved card-blocking,
credential-reset, account-security, and fraud-escalation procedures. These protective actions may need to occur before the full
dispute investigation is complete.
3.4 Acknowledge receipt
Provide the case reference, explain the next steps, indicate that evidence may be requested, and describe how updates will be
provided. Do not state that the claim has been accepted or that a refund is guaranteed.

Page 5
4. Triage, Deadlines and Evidence Collection
4.1 Triage
7. Assign a provisional dispute category based on the customer’s account and available transaction information.
8. Determine whether the transaction is pending, posted, reversed, refunded, or otherwise not yet eligible for the requested dispute
route.
9. Check the applicable customer terms, card-scheme requirements, legal obligations, and internal procedures for time limits and
required evidence.
10. Assign case priority according to risk, time remaining before a deadline, customer impact, and internal service targets.
11. Route potential fraud or account compromise to the appropriate team while retaining ownership or a tracked hand-off.
4.2 Deadline management

Deadlines vary by dispute type, transaction route, card scheme, jurisdiction, and case circumstances. The analyst must check the
current authoritative rule source used by the institution rather than rely on memory or a generic number of days.
• Record the relevant deadline, its source, and the date it was checked.
• Set reminders and escalation points before the deadline, leaving time for review and submission.
• If a deadline may have been missed, escalate promptly and document whether any permitted remedy remains available.
• Do not delay a case while waiting for optional evidence if mandatory action must occur earlier under policy.
4.3 Evidence request
Request only information relevant to the dispute category. Give the customer a clear description of what is needed, an approved

submission method, and a reasonable response date consistent with applicable rules.
4.4 Evidence examples
Dispute type Potentially relevant evidence
Unauthorised transaction Customer declaration, authentication records, device/session
indicators, card status, fraud monitoring results, and
transaction-channel data.
Duplicate charge Both transaction references, posting status, receipt, merchant
record, and reversal/refund information.
Incorrect amount Receipt, invoice, authorisation amount, posted amount,
currency conversion details, and merchant communication.
Refund not received Cancellation/return confirmation, merchant refund reference,
original transaction, and elapsed processing time.
Goods/services issue Order confirmation, delivery record, cancellation terms,

customer-merchant correspondence, and relevant proof of non-
receipt or mismatch.
ATM cash dispute ATM ID and location, transaction log, cash-dispense or reversal
records, and any available machine investigation result.

Page 6
5. Investigate the Transaction
5.1 Transaction-system review
12. Retrieve the transaction from the approved card-processing or core banking system.
13. Confirm whether it is authorised, posted, reversed, refunded, disputed previously, or linked to another transaction.
14. Compare the transaction date, amount, currency, merchant information, and reference with the customer’s account.
15. Review relevant available records for the transaction channel, such as chip/contactless, online, wallet, ATM, or other approved
channel data.
16. Check whether merchant credits, reversals, partial refunds, or currency-conversion differences explain the reported issue.
17. Record findings, sources consulted, and any limitations in the case notes.
5.2 Unauthorised transaction investigation

• Review authentication and transaction indicators available under approved access rights.
• Consider whether the customer reports loss of card, credential compromise, social engineering, or unfamiliar device activity.
• Check for related transactions or patterns that may require a broader fraud review.
• Apply the institution’s approved liability assessment; do not infer customer fault from a single indicator alone.
• Escalate where evidence is conflicting, fraud is ongoing, or specialist assessment is required.
5.3 Merchant-related investigation
• Check whether the customer attempted to resolve the issue with the merchant where this is relevant and required.
• Review order, cancellation, delivery, refund, or service records supplied by the customer.

• Distinguish a merchant disagreement from an unauthorised transaction; the applicable remedy may differ.
• Record unanswered evidence requests and any deadline implications.
5.4 Evidence integrity and privacy
Use only authorised sources. Preserve original documents or system references according to records policy, note when evidence was
received, and avoid changing source records. Share evidence externally only through approved channels and only when permitted.
5.5 Investigation outcome
Finding Next action
Evidence supports a valid dispute route Prepare a recommendation and required
submission/adjustment steps.
Evidence supports a merchant refund or reversal already
completed
Verify posting and explain the outcome to the customer, subject
to review.

Evidence is incomplete or conflicting Request relevant information or escalate; track deadline and
next action.
Potential fraud or broader control issue Refer to Fraud Operations and follow protective/incident
procedures.
No eligible remedy identified Document the policy/rule basis and prepare a clear customer
explanation, subject to required review.

Page 7
6. Determine Eligibility and Recommend an Outcome
6.1 Eligibility assessment
The analyst evaluates the case against the institution’s current approved dispute rules, card-scheme requirements, customer terms,
and applicable law. This SOP intentionally does not reproduce scheme-specific deadlines, reason codes, or legal tests, which can
change and must be checked in authoritative systems.
18. Confirm that the transaction and dispute category qualify for the proposed remedy.
19. Confirm the case is within the applicable time limit or identify an authorised exception route if one exists.
20. Check that mandatory evidence and customer declarations are present.
21. Review any merchant response, previous credit, reversal, partial refund, or duplicate case to prevent double recovery.

22. Calculate the proposed amount and determine whether the case is full, partial, or not eligible.
23. Write a concise recommendation with supporting facts, applicable rule reference, risks, and unresolved questions.
6.2 Decision options
Recommendation Conditions / action
Proceed with dispute / chargeback Eligibility and evidence support the route; submit through
approved systems before the deadline.
Request further evidence A relevant fact or required document is missing; specify owner
and response date.
Refer for specialist review Fraud, legal, compliance, complex liability, or policy ambiguity
requires authorised input.
Resolve through verified refund/reversal Confirm the entry is real and correctly posted before explaining
or closing the case.

Decline the claim Only after the required assessment and review; record the
evidence, rule basis, and customer communication plan.
6.3 Independent review
Where required by policy, a Checker or Supervisor independently reviews the category, deadline, evidence, rule basis, amount, and
proposed outcome. The reviewer should challenge gaps rather than merely confirm that fields are populated.
6.4 Decision record
• Case ID and transaction reference.
• Dispute category and applicable rule/source reference.
• Evidence considered and material facts established.
• Amount and proposed action.
• Reviewer identity, decision, date/time, and any conditions.
• Customer communication wording or approved template used.
6.5 Fair and consistent treatment

Apply the same approved criteria to comparable cases. If a decision differs from normal practice, document the material reason and
obtain required approval. Customer dissatisfaction alone must not cause a rule to be bypassed, and operational convenience must
not determine the outcome.

Page 8
7. Provisional Credit, Customer Communication and Submission
7.1 Provisional credit assessment
Some institutions or jurisdictions may require or permit temporary credit in defined circumstances. Determine eligibility, amount,
timing, disclosures, and approval requirements from the current approved policy and applicable law. Do not assume provisional credit
is automatic for every dispute.
24. Confirm the case meets the institution’s provisional-credit criteria, if applicable.
25. Calculate the amount based on the eligible disputed transaction and any prior refunds or reversals.
26. Obtain the required approval and create the credit through the approved system.
27. Clearly record whether the credit is provisional or final, the posting reference, and any conditions for reversal.

28. Track the case until a final decision determines whether further adjustment is required.
7.2 Customer updates
Use a verified contact channel and approved templates. Explain the current stage, any information needed, expected next update
where known, and how to contact the bank. Avoid disclosing confidential fraud controls, internal deliberations, or information
prohibited by law or policy.
7.3 Prepare and submit dispute
29. Confirm that the case is approved for submission and all required fields and evidence are complete.
30. Select the correct reason/category and required code in the authorised platform, using current authoritative guidance.
31. Attach evidence in the accepted format and verify that documents are legible and relevant.

32. Submit before the applicable deadline and capture the platform/network reference and timestamp.
33. Confirm that the platform accepted the submission; if the status is uncertain, investigate before retrying to avoid duplicate
submissions.
34. Update the case status, next expected action, and follow-up date.
7.4 Submission failure
If submission fails, record the error, time, and platform reference. Follow the approved retry or contingency procedure, contact
technical support if needed, and escalate deadline risk promptly. Never bypass mandatory evidence, approval, or security controls to
force a submission.
7.5 Customer communication outcomes
• Case received and under review.
• Additional evidence required.
• Temporary credit applied, where applicable, with its status clearly explained.

• Decision made and any adjustment posted or pending.
• Case delayed, escalated, or closed, using approved wording.

Page 9
8. Follow-up, Merchant Response and Case Closure
8.1 Follow-up monitoring
35. Review the case queue for approaching deadlines, outstanding evidence, and responses due from external parties.
36. Record incoming responses and documents promptly, linking them to the correct case.
37. Assess whether new evidence changes eligibility, the recommended outcome, or the amount.
38. Escalate missed service targets, deadline risks, and unresolved platform issues to the designated supervisor.
39. Maintain customer updates at the frequency required by policy and applicable service commitments.
8.2 Merchant response / representment
If the merchant or its bank challenges a submitted dispute, assess the response against the applicable current rules and the evidence

on file. Do not automatically accept or reject a response. Obtain additional evidence and specialist review where needed, and submit
a further response only if permitted, supported, and approved.
8.3 Final financial adjustment
40. Confirm the final decision and any required approval.
41. Check whether a provisional credit, merchant refund, reversal, or previous adjustment has already been posted.
42. Calculate the net amount due to or from the customer, avoiding duplicate credits or recoveries.
43. Post the authorised adjustment through the approved system and retain the posting reference.
44. Reconcile the adjustment to the dispute record and transaction ledger.
8.4 Final customer notification

Communicate the final outcome in plain language. State whether the dispute was accepted in full, accepted in part, or declined;
explain the material reason within permitted disclosure boundaries; confirm any adjustment and timing where known; and provide the
approved complaint or appeal route if available.
8.5 Closure criteria
• A final outcome is recorded, or the case is formally transferred to an owned and tracked process.
• Required submissions and responses are complete or the reason for stopping is documented.
• Any provisional or final credits, reversals, fees, or recoveries are correctly posted and reconciled.
• Customer communication is recorded.
• Evidence, decision rationale, approvals, and timestamps are retained.

• Open related fraud or security actions have a separate owner and reference.
8.6 Reopened cases
If new evidence arrives or an adjustment is reversed, reopen or create a linked case according to policy. Preserve the original history,
record the reason for reopening, reassess deadlines, and assign an owner.

Page 10
9. Exceptions, Records and Quality Assurance
9.1 Exception handling
Exception Immediate action Owner / closure evidence
Customer identity cannot be verified Do not disclose sensitive case details;
use approved verification route.
Customer Service; verification result
recorded.
Possible ongoing card fraud Apply approved protective measures and
refer to Fraud Operations.
Fraud Operations; incident/case
reference and actions logged.
Deadline at risk or missed Escalate immediately; check any
permitted remedy and document
rationale.
Disputes Supervisor; authorised decision
and deadline record.
Missing evidence Request relevant evidence; track due
date and any rule implications.
Disputes Analyst; request and follow-up
recorded.

Duplicate case or prior refund Pause duplicate adjustment; compare
linked references and entries.
Analyst / Reconciliation; verified
resolution.
System or submission outage Use approved contingency plan; log
incident and avoid blind resubmission.
Operations / IT; incident reference and
confirmed submission status.
Conflicting evidence or complex liability Hold the decision and refer to authorised
specialist.
Supervisor / Compliance / Legal as
applicable; written disposition.
Incorrect credit or posting Raise controlled correction request and
reconcile; do not erase audit history.
Payments / Finance; approved correction
and ledger evidence.
9.2 Records to retain
• Customer report, authentication record, and relevant declarations.

• Transaction details, investigation notes, and evidence sources.
• Evidence supplied by the customer or merchant and timestamps received.
• Deadline checks, reason/category references, recommendations, approvals, and decisions.
• Submission references, responses, credit/adjustment postings, and reconciliation evidence.
• Customer communications, escalations, complaints, and closure notes.
Retention periods, storage locations, access controls, and disposal methods must follow the bank’s approved records schedule and
applicable law. Do not save customer records in personal storage or unapproved applications.
9.3 Quality assurance and monitoring
• Sample cases for correct categorisation, evidence quality, deadline compliance, approval, and customer communication.

• Monitor time to first response, average resolution time, overdue cases, upheld/declined outcomes, reopened cases, adjustment
errors, and complaint trends.
• Analyse root causes and improve forms, validation, training, system rules, and customer guidance through formal change
management.
9.4 End-of-case checklist
• Customer identity verified and case reference created.
• Transaction status and dispute category confirmed.
• Applicable deadline and evidence requirements checked.
• Fraud/protection concerns handled and escalated where needed.
• Investigation and decision rationale documented.
• Required independent approval obtained.
• Submission, provisional/final credit, or other remedy correctly processed.
• Customer notified through a verified channel.

• Financial entries reconciled and records retained.
• Open related actions assigned to an owner with a tracking reference.
10. Governance and Change History
Before adapting this training draft for operational use, obtain review from Card Operations, Fraud Operations, Compliance, Legal,
Customer Experience, Technology, and Records Management as relevant. Review it whenever card-scheme rules, legal
requirements, product terms, systems, or internal controls change.
